theory.intro: The graph of $y=f^{-1}(x)$ is the graph of an existing one-to-one branch of $y=f(x)$ reflected in the line $y=x$. At a corresponding interior point where the original derivative is finite and nonzero, reflecting a tangent of gradient $m$ produces a tangent of gradient $\dfrac{1}{m}$, so the two derivatives are reciprocals.
facts: For an existing inverse branch, at a corresponding interior point where $f'$ is finite and nonzero, the rule is $\left(f^{-1}\right)'(x)=\dfrac{1}{f'\left(f^{-1}(x)\right)}$, usually used as $\left(f^{-1}\right)'(b)=\dfrac{1}{f'(a)}$.
Evaluate $f'$ at $a$, the input of $f$, and never at $b$.
Under the same conditions, in Leibniz notation the rule reads $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{1}{dx/dy}$, where $y$ is the inverse function.

If a differentiable one-to-one branch has a horizontal tangent at $(a,b)$, its reflection has a vertical tangent at $(b,a)$, so no finite inverse derivative exists there. This can be an endpoint tangent; $f'(a)=0$ alone does not ensure an inverse branch exists.
The inverse exists only where $f$ is one-to-one, so restrict the domain of $f$ when necessary.
The domain of $f^{-1}$ is the range of $f$, and outside that domain no gradient exists.
You may instead find $f^{-1}(x)$ explicitly and differentiate it directly; the two methods agree where the reciprocal rule applies.
steps: Identify the pair: find the value $a$ with $f(a)=b$, so that $f^{-1}(b)=a$.

Check that the inverse branch exists and $a$ is an interior point with a finite nonzero derivative, then evaluate $f'(a)$ and take its reciprocal: $\left(f^{-1}\right)'(b)=\dfrac{1}{f'(a)}$. Treat endpoints and zero derivatives separately.

workedExamples.solution_text:
Swap $x$ and $y$ and make $y$ the subject.
$\begin{align*}x&=y^{3}+6\\y^{3}&=x-6\\f^{-1}(x)&=\sqrt[3]{x-6}\\\left(f^{-1}\right)'(x)&=\frac{1}{3(x-6)^{2/3}},\qquad x\ne6\end{align*}$
At $x=6$, the inverse has a vertical tangent and no finite derivative.

workedExamples.question_text: Let $f(x)=x^{2}-8$ for $x\ge0$. Find its inverse, stating its domain, and differentiate the inverse wherever its ordinary derivative exists.
workedExamples.solution_text:
$\begin{align*}x&=y^{2}-8\\y^{2}&=x+8\end{align*}$
The inverse takes values $y\ge0$, so choose the positive square root.
$\begin{align*}f^{-1}(x)&=\sqrt{x+8},\qquad x\ge-8\\\left(f^{-1}\right)'(x)&=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x+8}},\qquad x>-8\end{align*}$
At $x=-8$, the inverse has a vertical endpoint tangent and no finite derivative.

workedExamples.question_text: Let $f(x)=x^{3}+6x$. Given $f(1)=7$, find the gradient of the tangent to $y=f^{-1}(x)$ at $(7,1)$.
Let $f(x)=x\ln x$ for $x>e^{-1}$. Find the gradient of the tangent to $y=f^{-1}(x)$ at $(e,e)$.
workedExamples.solution_text:
$f(e)=e\ln e=e$, so $f^{-1}(e)=e$.
Use the product rule to differentiate $f$.
$\begin{align*}f'(x)&=\ln x+x\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)\\&=\ln x+1\\f'(e)&=2\\\left(f^{-1}\right)'(e)&=\frac{1}{f'(e)}\\&=\frac{1}{2}\end{align*}$

workedExamples.question_text: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{3x+2}{x+4}$. Find the gradient of the tangent to $y=f^{-1}(x)$ at $\left(-\dfrac{1}{3},-1\right)$.
workedExamples.solution_text:
$f(-1)=\dfrac{-3+2}{-1+4}=-\dfrac{1}{3}$, so $f^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{1}{3}\right)=-1$.
Use the quotient rule, then take the reciprocal.
$\begin{align*}f'(x)&=\frac{3(x+4)-(3x+2)}{(x+4)^{2}}\\&=\frac{10}{(x+4)^{2}}\\f'(-1)&=\frac{10}{9}\\\left(f^{-1}\right)'\left(-\frac{1}{3}\right)&=\frac{1}{f'(-1)}\\&=\frac{9}{10}\end{align*}$

workedExamples.question_text: Let $f(x)=x^{4}e^{x}$ for $x\ge0$. Write the inverse relation as $x=f(y)$ and find $\dfrac{dx}{dy}$ in terms of $y$.
workedExamples.solution_text:
Swap $x$ and $y$, then use the product rule.
$\begin{align*}x&=y^{4}e^{y}\\\frac{dx}{dy}&=4y^{3}e^{y}+y^{4}e^{y}\\&=y^{3}e^{y}(4+y)\end{align*}$
This is $dx/dy$ for the swapped relation, before taking a reciprocal.

workedExamples.question_text: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{5x-2}{2x+3}$. Write the inverse relation as $x=f(y)$ and find $\dfrac{dx}{dy}$ in terms of $y$.
workedExamples.solution_text:
Swap $x$ and $y$, then use the quotient rule.
$\begin{align*}x&=\frac{5y-2}{2y+3}\\\frac{dx}{dy}&=\frac{5(2y+3)-2(5y-2)}{(2y+3)^{2}}\\&=\frac{19}{(2y+3)^{2}},\qquad y\ne-\frac{3}{2}\end{align*}$

workedExamples.question_text: Let $f(x)=x^{3}-3x+8$ for $-1\le x\le1$. The point $(6,1)$ lies on $y=f^{-1}(x)$. Explain why the inverse has no finite tangent gradient there.
workedExamples.solution_text:
$f'(x)=3x^{2}-3<0$ for $-1<x<1$, so the given branch is strictly decreasing and has an inverse.
$\begin{align*}f(1)&=1-3+8=6\\f'(1)&=3-3=0\end{align*}$
The original branch has a horizontal endpoint tangent at $(1,6)$. Reflection in $y=x$ gives a vertical endpoint tangent at $(6,1)$, so the inverse has no finite derivative there.

workedExamples.question_text: Let $f(x)=\sqrt{x-7}+2$. Find the gradient of $y=f^{-1}(x)$ at $x=-1$, or explain why it does not exist.
workedExamples.solution_text:
The range of $f$ is $[2,\infty)$, so the domain of $f^{-1}$ is $[2,\infty)$.
Since $-1$ is outside this domain, there is no corresponding point on the inverse and no gradient.

workedExamples.question_text:
Let $f(x)=\sqrt{x-6}$ for $x\ge6$.
a. Find $f^{-1}(x)$ and state its domain.
b. For $x>0$, differentiate the inverse using the reciprocal rule and verify the result directly.
workedExamples.solution_text:
a. Swap $x$ and $y$.
$\begin{align*}x&=\sqrt{y-6}\\x^{2}&=y-6\\f^{-1}(x)&=x^{2}+6\end{align*}$
Its domain is $x\ge0$, the range of $f$.

b. $f'(t)=\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{t-6}}$ for $t>6$.
For $x>0$:
$\begin{align*}\left(f^{-1}\right)'(x)&=\frac{1}{f'\left(f^{-1}(x)\right)}\\&=\frac{1}{\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x^{2}+6-6}}}\\&=2x\end{align*}$
Direct differentiation gives the same result:
$\frac{d}{dx}(x^{2}+6)=2x$.
At $x=0$, the reciprocal rule does not apply because $f'(6)$ is undefined. The inverse has right derivative $0$ there; an ordinary two-sided derivative is not defined at this endpoint.

workedExamples.question_text: Let $f(x)=x(3x-2)^{4}$ for $x\ge1$, a strictly increasing branch. Write the inverse relation as $x=f(y)$ and find $\dfrac{dx}{dy}$ in terms of $y$.
workedExamples.solution_text:
Swap $x$ and $y$. Use the product rule and include the chain-rule factor $3$ when differentiating $(3y-2)^{4}$.
$\begin{align*}x&=y(3y-2)^{4}\\\frac{dx}{dy}&=(3y-2)^{4}+y\cdot4(3y-2)^{3}\cdot3\\&=(3y-2)^{3}\bigl((3y-2)+12y\bigr)\\&=(3y-2)^{3}(15y-2),\qquad y\ge1\end{align*}$

foundation.solution_text:
$y=x^{5}-2$
Swapping $x$ and $y$: $x=y^{5}-2$
$y=(x+2)^{\frac{1}{5}}$
$f^{-1}(x)=(x+2)^{\frac{1}{5}}$
$\left(f^{-1}\right)'(x)=\dfrac{1}{5}(x+2)^{-\frac{4}{5}}$ for $x\ne-2$.
At $x=-2$, the inverse has a vertical tangent and its derivative is undefined.

development.question_text:
Let $f(x)=x^{3}e^{x}$ for $x\ge0$.
Find $\dfrac{dx}{dy}$ for the inverse function $f^{-1}$, in terms of $y$.

Let $f(x)=\dfrac{2x-1}{x+3}$.
Find $\dfrac{dx}{dy}$ for the inverse function $f^{-1}$, in terms of $y$.

Let $y=x\cos 2x$ for $\dfrac{\pi}{4}\le x\le\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, on which the function is strictly decreasing.
Find $\dfrac{dx}{dy}$ for the inverse function, in terms of $y$.

development.solution_text:
$y=x^{2}+5$
Swapping $x$ and $y$: $x=y^{2}+5$
$y^{2}=x-5$
Since the domain of $f$ is $x\ge 0$, take $y=\sqrt{x-5}$.
$f^{-1}(x)=\sqrt{x-5}$ for $x\ge 5$
$\left(f^{-1}\right)'(x)=\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{x-5}}$ for $x>5$.
At $x=5$, the inverse has a vertical endpoint tangent and its derivative is undefined.

development.question_text:
Let $f(x)=\dfrac{x-1}{x+1}$.
The point $\left(\dfrac{1}{3},2\right)$ lies on $y=f^{-1}(x)$.
Find the gradient of the tangent to $y=f^{-1}(x)$ at that point.

Let $f(x)=x^{2}\ln x$ for $x>e^{-\frac{1}{2}}$, the increasing branch containing $e$.
The point $\left(e^{2},e\right)$ lies on $y=f^{-1}(x)$.
Find the gradient of the tangent to $y=f^{-1}(x)$ at that point.

Let $f(x)=x^{3}-3x+5$ for $-1\le x\le1$, a strictly decreasing branch ending at $x=1$.
The point $(3,1)$ lies on $y=f^{-1}(x)$.
Find the gradient of the tangent to $y=f^{-1}(x)$ at that point, or explain why it does not exist.
development.solution_text:
$(3,1)$ on $f^{-1}$ means $f(1)=3$, and $1-3+5=3$.
$f'(x)=3x^{2}-3$
$f'(1)=0$
The chosen branch has a horizontal endpoint tangent at $(1,3)$.
Its reflection is a vertical endpoint tangent at $(3,1)$, so $\left(f^{-1}\right)'(3)$ has no finite value.

development.question_text:
Let $f(x)=\sqrt{x-2}+1$.
Find the gradient of the tangent to $y=f^{-1}(x)$ at $x=-3$, or explain why it does not exist.
development.solution_text:
The range of $f$ is $y\ge 1$.
The domain of $f^{-1}$ is the range of $f$, so it is $x\ge 1$.
$x=-3$ lies outside this domain, so no point of $y=f^{-1}(x)$ has $x=-3$ and the gradient does not exist.

development.question_text:
Let $f(x)=\sqrt{x-4}$ for $x\ge 4$.
Show that $f^{-1}(x)=x^{2}+4$ for $x\ge 0$, then find $\left(f^{-1}\right)'(x)$ for $x>0$ using the formula $\left(f^{-1}\right)'(x)=\dfrac{1}{f'\left(f^{-1}(x)\right)}$.
development.solution_text:
$y=\sqrt{x-4}$
Swapping $x$ and $y$: $x=\sqrt{y-4}$
$x^{2}=y-4$
$f^{-1}(x)=x^{2}+4$, with domain $x\ge 0$, the range of $f$.
$f'(x)=\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{x-4}}$ for $x>4$.
For $x>0$, $\left(f^{-1}\right)'(x)=\dfrac{1}{f'\left(x^{2}+4\right)}$
$=\dfrac{1}{\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x^{2}+4-4}}}$
$=2x$
At $x=0$, the reciprocal formula does not apply because $f'(4)$ is undefined. Directly from $f^{-1}(x)=x^{2}+4$, the endpoint right derivative is $0$; an ordinary two-sided derivative is not defined there.

mastery.question_text:
Let $f(x)=x^{3}+x-1$.
The point $(9,2)$ lies on $y=f^{-1}(x)$.
Find $\left(f^{-1}\right)'(9)$.

Let $f(x)=2x+\sin x$.
The point $(2\pi,\pi)$ lies on $y=f^{-1}(x)$.
Find $\left(f^{-1}\right)'(2\pi)$.

mastery.solution_text:
$y=x^{2}-6x+11=(x-3)^{2}+2$
Swapping $x$ and $y$: $x=(y-3)^{2}+2$
$(y-3)^{2}=x-2$
Since $x\ge 3$ for $f$, its inverse takes values $y\ge 3$, so $y-3=\sqrt{x-2}$.
$f^{-1}(x)=3+\sqrt{x-2}$ for $x\ge 2$
$\left(f^{-1}\right)'(x)=\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{x-2}}$ for $x>2$.
At $x=2$, the inverse has a vertical endpoint tangent and its derivative is undefined.
